title: Reading in Translation
objective: After this level you can weigh how two translations of the same passage can give a reader different pictures.
summary: Butler's prose Odyssey (1900) keeps Homer's repeated formulas; Pope's rhymed one (1725 to 1726) varies them. One Greek word, polytropos, gives several Odysseuses.

cards.headline: The same Greek sunrise, in two English versions.
cards.body: Book II of the Odyssey opens at dawn. Samuel Butler's translation: "Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared". Alexander Pope's: "Now reddening from the dawn, the morning ray / Glow'd in the front of heaven". Same Greek. Two different mornings.

cards.headline: Prose or rhyme
cards.body: Butler's Odyssey, first published in 1900, is in plain English prose. He admitted the cost: much that is right in poetry, he wrote, is wrong in prose. Pope's Odyssey (1725 to 1726), a job he shared with William Broome and Elijah Fenton, is in rhyming heroic couplets of 10-syllable lines. Each choice gains something and gives something up.

cards.headline: One word, several heroes
cards.body: The first line calls Odysseus polytropos. The word can mean much-travelled or much-wandering, or, figuratively, turning many ways: versatile, wily. Butler writes "that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide", keeping both senses. Pope opens with "The man for wisdom's various arts renown'd", the clever man first, and brings in "Wandering from clime to clime" a few lines later. Neither is wrong. Each hands you a slightly different Odysseus.

cards.fact: Butler keeps Homer's repeated dawn. Pope varies it.
cards.context: In Butler, "the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" comes back again and again, so you can watch the oral poet's building blocks at work. Pope renders the same dawn in varying words rather than one fixed phrase: Book II opens with "Now reddening from the dawn". Beautiful, but the repeated formula is harder to spot.

cards.headline: Two Odysseys: compared
learned: Butler: prose, with the formulas left visible
Pope: rhyming couplets, with the wording varied
Every translation chooses what to keep

questions.prompt: Which form did Samuel Butler choose for his 1900 Odyssey?
questions.explanation: Butler rendered the Odyssey into English prose, admitting that much that is right in poetry is wrong in prose.

questions.prompt: Homer calls Odysseus polytropos. Why might a reader of Butler's first line picture a different hero from a reader of Pope's?

options.label: Pope translated the word as "sailor"
options.rationale: Pope writes of wisdom's various arts.

options.label: Butler invented the wandering; Homer never implies it
options.rationale: The Greek word can mean much-wandering.

options.label: They translated from two different Greek poems
options.rationale: Both translate the same first line.

options.label: Butler keeps both senses; Pope's first line stresses cleverness

questions.explanation: Polytropos can mean much-wandering or wily. Butler's "ingenious hero who travelled far and wide" keeps both; Pope's first line leads with cleverness.

questions.prompt: Level 6 said formulas like "rosy-fingered dawn" are clues to how Homer's poems were composed. In which translation is that clue easier to see?

options.label: Pope's, which varies the wording
options.rationale: Varying the words hides the repetition.

options.label: Neither: no translation keeps formulas
options.rationale: Butler's keeps this one again and again.

options.label: Both equally, since they translate the same poem

questions.explanation: Butler repeats "the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" again and again, so the oral formula stays visible; Pope varies it.
